\begin{itemize}
Item (1) is immediate from the relations $\ell_+(x,\lambda \xi)=\frac{1}{\lambda}\ell_+(x,\xi)$ and $\gamma_{x,\lambda \xi}(t)=\gamma_{x,\xi}(\lambda t)$ for any $\lambda>0$. Then 
$$
u(x,\lambda \xi)=\int_0^{\frac{1}{\lambda}\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(\lambda t)) dt = \frac{1}{\lambda} u(x,\xi).
 $$
Prove item (2). For $s \in \mathbb{R}$ sufficiently small, we set  $x_s=\gamma_{x,\xi}(s)$ and $\xi_s=\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(s).$ Then, $\gamma_{x_s,\xi_s}(t)=\gamma_{x,\xi}(t+s)$ and $\ell_+(x_s,\xi_s)=\tau_+(x,\xi)-s.$ So,
$$
 u(\gamma_{x,\xi}(s),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(s))=u(x_s,\xi_s) = \int_0^{\ell_+(x_s,\xi_s)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t+s)) dt =\int_s^{\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)) dt .
$$
 Differentiating with respect to $s$ and taking $s=0$, we obtain that 
 $$
 \frac{\partial u}{\partial x_i}\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}^i(0)+\frac{\partial u}{\partial \xi_i}  \ddot {\gamma}_{x,\xi}^{i}(0)=-f(x).
 $$
 Since we have $\gamma_{x,\xi}(0)=x$, $\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(0)=\xi$ and $\ddot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}^{i}(0)=-\Gamma ^i_{jk}(x)\xi^j\xi^k,$ then $$\xi^i\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_i}-\Gamma^i_{jk}\xi^j\xi^k\frac{\partial u}{\partial \xi_i}= -f(x).$$ Thus we have $Hu=-f$.\\
To prove item (3), applying the operator $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}$ to the kinetic equation, we obtain $ \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} (Hu)=-\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} f= 0.$ It follows that 
$$
 0= \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} (Hu)  = \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_j (\xi^i  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_i u) dx^j  =(\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_j \xi^i ) \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_i u dx^j+\xi ^i  (\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_j \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_i u) dx^j.
$$
From (\ref{2.24}) and (\ref{2.25}), we get 
$$
0=\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u+H(\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}u).
$$
\end{itemize}
The proof is complete.

\begin{equation}\label{4.3}
u_2(x,t)=(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_{2,h}(x,t),
\end{equation}
to the wave equation corresponding to the coefficients $a_2$ and $q_2$,
$$

$$
where $r_{2,h}$ satisfies
\begin{gather}\label{4.4}
h^{-1}\norm{r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{\partial_t r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{\nabla r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)},
\\ \nonumber
r_{2,h}(x,t)=0,\quad\forall (x,t)\in\,\Sigma.
\end{gather}
Moreover
$$
u_2\in  \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\mathrm{M})) \cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})).
$$

$$
f_h(x,t)=(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h},\quad  (x,t)\in\Sigma,
$$

$$

w(x,0)=\partial_tw(x,0)=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, \mathrm{M},\cr

H^1_0(\mathrm{M})).

  $$

nodes.name: Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold
nodes.statement: Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold setcounterequation0 The geodesic X-ray transform of a function is defined by integrating over geodesics. It is naturally arises in linearization of the problem of determining a coefficient in partial differential equation. The X-ray transform also arises in Computer Tomography, Positron Emission Tomography, geophysical imaging in determining the inner structure of the Earth, ultrasound imaging. Uniqueness result and stability estimates of the geodesic X-ray transform were obtained by Mukhometov for simple surface. For simple manifolds of any dimension this result was proven in , , see also V. A. Sharafutdinov's book . In his paper Dairbekov generalized this result for nontrapping manifolds without conjugate points . Fredholm type inversion formulas were given in by Pestov and Uhlmann. In this section we first collect some formulas needed in the rest of this paper and introduce the geodesical X-ray transform on the manifolds we will be using. Let (M,g) be a Riemannian manifold, for xin M and xiin T_xM we let gamma_x,xi denote the unique geodesic starting at the point x in the direction xi. By SM=set(x,xi)in TM;\,absxi=1, S^*M=set(x,p)in T^*M;\,absp=1, we denote the sphere bundle and co-sphere bundle of M. The exponential map exp_x:T_xMto M is given by exp_x(v)=gamma_x,xi(absv), xi=fracv\,\,absv. A compact Riemannian manifold (M,\, g) with boundary is called a convex non-trapping manifold, if it satisfies two conditions: item[(i)] the boundary partial M is strictly convex, i.e., the second fundamental form of the boundary is positive definite at every boundary point, item[(ii)] all geodesics having finite length in M, i.e., for each (x,xi) in SM, the maximal geodesic gamma_x,xi(t) satisfying the initial conditions gamma_x,xi(0) = x and dotgamma_x,xi(0) = xi is defined on a finite segment with extremities ell_-(x,xi) and ell_+(x,xi). We recall that a geodesic gamma: [a, b] longrightarrow M is maximal if it cannot be extended to a segment [a-varepsilon_1, b+varepsilon_2], where varepsilon_i geq 0 and varepsilon_1 + varepsilon_2 > 0. An important subclass of convex non-trapping manifolds are simple manifolds. We say that a compact Riemannian manifold (M, g) is simple if it satisfies the following properties item[(a)] (M,g) is convex and non-trapping, item[(b)] there are no conjugate points on any geodesic. A simple n-dimensional Riemannian manifold is diffeomorphic to a closed ball in R^n, and any pair of points in the manifold are joined by an unique geodesic. Let (x,xi)in SM, there exist a unique geodesic gamma_x,xi associated to (x,xi) which is maxmimally defined on a finite intervall [ell_-(x,xi),ell_+(x,xi)], with gamma_x,xi(ell_pm(x,xi))inpartialM. We define the geodesic flow phi_t as following phi_t:SMto SM, phi_t(x,xi)=(gamma_x,xi(t),dotgamma_x,xi(t)), tin [ell_-(x,xi),ell_+(x,xi)], and phi_t is a flow, that is, phi_tcircphi_s=phi_t+s. Now, we introduce the submanifolds of inner and outer vectors of SM partial_pmSM =set(x,xi)in SM,\, x in partial M,\, pmseqxi,nu(x)< 0, where nu is the unit outer normal to the boundary. Note that the manifolds partial_+ SM and partial_-SM have the same boundary S(partial M), and partial SM = partial_+ SMcup partial_- SM. We denote by C^infty(partial_+ SM) be space of smooth functions on the manifold partial_+SM. Thus we can define two functions ell_pm:SMtoR which satisfy ell_-(x,xi)leq 0, ell_+(x,xi)geq 0, ell_+(x,xi)=-ell_-(x,-xi), ell_-(x,xi)=0, (x,xi)inpartial_+SM, ell_+(x,xi)=0, (x,xi)inpartial_-SM, ell_-(phi_t(x,xi))=ell_-(x,xi)-t, ell_+(phi_t(x,xi))=ell_+(x,xi)-t. For (x,xi)inpartial_+ SM, we denote by gamma_x,xi : [0,ell_+(x,xi)] to M the maximal geodesic satisfying the initial conditions gamma_x,xi(0) = x and dotgamma_x,xi(0) = xi. Concerning smoothness properties of ell_pm(x,xi), we can see that these functions are smooth near a point (x,xi) such that the geodesic gamma_x,xi(t) intersects partialM transversely for t=ell_pm(x,xi). By strict convexity of partialM, the functions ell_pm(x,xi) are smooth on TM setminus T(partialM). In fact, all points of TM cap T(partialM) are singular for ell_pm; since some derivatives of these functions are unbounded in a neighbourhood of such points. In particular, ell_+ is smooth on partial_+SM, see Lemma 4.1.1 of . The Riemannian scalar product on T_xM induces the volume form on S_xM, denoted by d omega_x(xi) and given by d omega_x(xi)=sqrtabsg \, sum_k=1^n(-1)^kxi^k d xi^1wedgecdotswedge widehatd xi^kwedgecdotswedge d xi^n. As usual, the notation \, widehatcdot \, means that the corresponding factor has been dropped. We introduce the volume form \,dv^2n-1 on the manifold SM by \,dv^2n-1 (x,xi)=domega_x(xi)wedge \,dv^n, where \,dv^n is the Riemannnian volume form on M. By Liouville's theorem, the form \,dv^2n-1 is preserved by the geodesic flow. The corresponding volume form on the boundary partial SM =set(x,xi)in SM,\, xinpartial M is given by \,dsigma^2n-2=domega_x(xi) wedge \,dsigma^n-1, where \,dsigma^n-1 is the volume form of partial M. Let L^2_mu(partial_+SM) be the space of square integrable functions with respect to the measure mu(x,xi)\,dsigma^2n-2 with mu(x,xi)=absseqxi,nu(x). This Hilbert space is endowed with the scalar product parau,v_mu=int_partial_+SMu(x,xi) overlinev(x,xi) mu(x,xi)\,dsigma^2n-2. The ray transform (also called geodesic X-ray transform) on a convex non trapping manifold M is the linear operator I:C^infty(M)longrightarrow C^infty(partial_+SM), defined by the equality I f(x,xi)=int_0^ell_+(x,xi)f(gamma_x,xi(t))\, d t, (x,xi)inpartial_+SM. The right-hand side of () is a smooth function on partial_+SM because the integration limit ell_+(x,xi) is a smooth function on partial_+SM. The ray transform on a convex non trapping manifold M can be extended as a bounded operator I:H^k(M)longrightarrow H^k(partial_+SM), for every integer kgeq 1, see Theorem 4.2.1 of .

nodes.raw_latex:
Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold
\setcounter{equation}{0}


The geodesic $X$-ray transform of a function is defined by integrating over geodesics.
It is naturally arises in linearization of the problem of determining a coefficient in partial differential equation. The $X$-ray transform also
arises in Computer Tomography, Positron Emission Tomography, geophysical imaging
in determining the inner structure of the Earth, ultrasound imaging. Uniqueness
result and stability estimates of the geodesic $X$-ray transform were obtained by Mukhometov \cite{[Mukh]} for simple surface. For simple manifolds of any dimension this
result was proven in \cite{[SU2]}, \cite{[SU3]}, see also V. A. Sharafutdinov's book \cite{[Sh]}. In his paper Dairbekov generalized this result for nontrapping manifolds without conjugate points \cite{[Dai]}. Fredholm type inversion formulas were given in \cite{[PU]} by Pestov and Uhlmann.
\medskip

In this section we first collect some  formulas needed in the rest of this paper and introduce the geodesical $X$-ray transform on the manifolds we will be using. Let $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ be a Riemannian manifold, for $x\in \mathrm{M}$ and $\xi\in T_x\mathrm{M}$ we let  $\gamma_{x,\xi}$ denote the unique geodesic starting at the point $x$ in the direction $\xi$.  By
\begin{align*}
S\mathrm{M}=\set{(x,\xi)\in T\mathrm{M};\,\abs{\xi}=1}, \quad
S^*\mathrm{M}=\set{(x,p)\in T^*\mathrm{M};\,\abs{p}=1},
\end{align*}
we denote the sphere bundle and co-sphere bundle of $\mathrm{M}$. The exponential map $\exp_x:T_x\mathrm{M}\to \mathrm{M}$ is given by
\begin{equation}\label{2.1}
\exp_x(v)=\gamma_{x,\xi}(\abs{v}),\quad \xi=\frac{v\,\,}{\abs{v}}.
\end{equation}
A compact Riemannian manifold $(\mathrm{M},\, \mathrm{g})$ with boundary is called a convex non-trapping
manifold, if it satisfies two conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] the boundary $\partial \mathrm{M}$ is strictly convex, i.e., the second fundamental form of the boundary is positive definite at every
    boundary point,
    \item[(ii)] all geodesics having finite length in $\mathrm{M}$, i.e., for each $(x,\xi) \in S\mathrm{M}$, the maximal
    geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)$ satisfying the initial conditions $\gamma_{x,\xi}(0) = x$ and $\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(0) = \xi$ is defined on
    a finite segment with extremities $\ell_{-}(x,\xi)$ and $\ell_{+}(x,\xi)$. We recall that a geodesic $\gamma: [a, b] \longrightarrow M$ is maximal
    if it cannot be extended to a segment $[a-\varepsilon_1, b+\varepsilon_2]$, where $\varepsilon_i \geq 0$ and $\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 > 0$.
\end{enumerate}
An important subclass of convex non-trapping manifolds are simple manifolds. We say that a compact Riemannian
manifold $(\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{g})$ is simple if it satisfies the following properties
\begin{enumerate}
     \item[(a)] $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ is convex and non-trapping, 
     \item[(b)] there are no conjugate points on any geodesic.
\end{enumerate}
A simple $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold is diffeomorphic to a closed ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and any pair of
points in the manifold are joined by an unique geodesic.
\medskip

Let $(x,\xi)\in S\mathrm{M}$, there exist a unique geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}$ associated to $(x,\xi)$ which is maxmimally defined on a finite intervall $[\ell_-(x,\xi),\ell_+(x,\xi)]$, with $\gamma_{x,\xi}(\ell_\pm(x,\xi))\in\partial\mathrm{M}$. We define the geodesic flow $\phi_t$ as following
\begin{equation}\label{2.2}
\phi_t:S\mathrm{M}\to S\mathrm{M},\quad \phi_t(x,\xi)=(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(t)),\quad t\in [\ell_-(x,\xi),\ell_+(x,\xi)],
\end{equation}
and $\phi_t$ is a flow, that is, $\phi_t\circ\phi_s=\phi_{t+s}$.
\smallskip

Now, we introduce the submanifolds of inner and outer vectors of $S\mathrm{M}$
\begin{equation}\label{2.3}
\partial_{\pm}S\mathrm{M} =\set{(x,\xi)\in S\mathrm{M},\, x \in \partial \mathrm{M},\, \pm\seq{\xi,\nu(x)}< 0},
\end{equation}
where $\nu$ is the unit outer normal to the boundary. Note that the manifolds $\partial_+ S\mathrm{M}$ and $\partial_-S\mathrm{M}$ have the same boundary $S(\partial \mathrm{M})$, and $\partial S\mathrm{M} = \partial_+ S\mathrm{M}\cup \partial_- S\mathrm{M}$. We denote by  $\mathcal{C}^\infty(\partial_+ S\mathrm{M})$ be space of smooth functions on the manifold $\partial_+S\mathrm{M}$. Thus we can define two functions $\ell_\pm:S\mathrm{M}\to\mathbb{R}$ which satisfy
$$
\ell_-(x,\xi)\leq 0,\quad \ell_+(x,\xi)\geq 0,\quad \ell_+(x,\xi)=-\ell_-(x,-\xi),
$$
$$
\ell_-(x,\xi)=0,\quad (x,\xi)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M},\quad \ell_+(x,\xi)=0,\quad (x,\xi)\in\partial_-S\mathrm{M},
$$
$$
\ell_-(\phi_t(x,\xi))=\ell_-(x,\xi)-t,\quad \ell_+(\phi_t(x,\xi))=\ell_+(x,\xi)-t.
$$
For $(x,\xi)\in\partial_+ S\mathrm{M}$,  we denote by $\gamma_{x,\xi} : [0,\ell_+(x,\xi)] \to \mathrm{M}$ the maximal
geodesic satisfying the initial conditions $\gamma_{x,\xi}(0) = x$ and $\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(0) = \xi$.

\smallskip

Concerning smoothness properties of  $\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$, we can see that these functions are smooth near a point $(x,\xi)$ such that the geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)$ intersects $\partial\mathrm{M}$ transversely for $t=\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$. By strict convexity of $\partial\mathrm{M}$, the functions $\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$ are smooth on $T\mathrm{M} \setminus T(\partial\mathrm{M}).$ In fact, all points of $T\mathrm{M} \cap T(\partial\mathrm{M})$ are singular for $\ell_{\pm}$; since some derivatives of these functions are unbounded in a neighbourhood of such points. In particular, $\ell_{+}$ is smooth on $\partial_+SM$, see Lemma 4.1.1 of \cite{[Sh]}.
\smallskip


The Riemannian scalar product on $T_x\mathrm{M}$ induces the volume form on $S_x\mathrm{M}$,
denoted by $\mathrm{d} \omega_x(\xi)$ and given by
$$
\mathrm{d} \omega_x(\xi)=\sqrt{\abs{\mathrm{g}}} \, \sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^k\xi^k \mathrm{d} \xi^1\wedge\cdots\wedge \widehat{\mathrm{d} \xi^k}\wedge\cdots\wedge \mathrm{d} \xi^n.
$$
As usual, the notation $\, \widehat{\cdot} \,$ means that the corresponding factor has been dropped.
We introduce the volume form $\,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}$ on the manifold $S\mathrm{M}$ by
$$
\,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} (x,\xi)=\mathrm{d}\omega_x(\xi)\wedge \,\mathrm{dv}^{n},
$$
where $\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}$ is the Riemannnian volume form on $\mathrm{M}$. By Liouville's theorem, the form $\,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}$ is preserved by the geodesic flow. The
corresponding volume form on the boundary $\partial S\mathrm{M} =\set{(x,\xi)\in S\mathrm{M},\, x\in\partial \mathrm{M}}$ is given
by
$$
\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}=\mathrm{d}\omega_x(\xi) \wedge \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1},
$$
where $\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1}$ is the volume form of $\partial \mathrm{M}$.
\smallskip


Let $L^2_\mu(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})$ be the space of square integrable functions with respect to the measure $\mu(x,\xi)\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}$ with
$\mu(x,\xi)=\abs{\seq{\xi,\nu(x)}}$. This Hilbert space is endowed with the scalar product
\begin{equation}\label{2.4}
\para{u,v}_\mu=\int_{\partial_+S\mathrm{M}}u(x,\xi) \overline{v}(x,\xi) \mu(x,\xi)\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}.
\end{equation}
The ray transform (also called geodesic $X$-ray transform) on a convex non trapping manifold $\mathrm{M}$ is the linear operator
\begin{equation}\label{2.5}
\mathcal{I}:\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathrm{M})\longrightarrow \mathcal{C}^\infty(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}),
\end{equation}
defined by the equality
\begin{equation}\label{2.6}
\mathcal{I} f(x,\xi)=\int_0^{\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t))\, \mathrm{d} t,\quad (x,\xi)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}.
\end{equation}
The right-hand side of (\ref{2.6}) is a smooth function on $\partial_+S\mathrm{M}$ because the integration limit $\ell_+(x,\xi)$ is a smooth function on $\partial_+S\mathrm{M}$.
The ray transform on a convex non trapping manifold $\mathrm{M}$ can be extended as a bounded operator
\begin{equation}\label{2.7}
\mathcal{I}:H^k(\mathrm{M})\longrightarrow H^k(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}),
\end{equation}
for every integer $k\geq 1$, see Theorem 4.2.1 of \cite{[Sh]}.
\medskip

The main purpose of this section is to present a preliminary estimate, which relates the

As before, we let $a_1,\,a_2\in\mathscr{A}(m_1,\eta)$ and $q_1,q_2\in\mathscr{Q}(m_2)$ such that $a_1=a_2$, $q_1=q_2$ near  the boundary $\partial\mathrm{M}$. We set
$$
a(x)=(a_1-a_2)(x),\quad q(x)=(q_1-q_2)(x).
$$
Recall that we have extended $a_{1},a_{2}$ as $W^{2,\infty}(\mathrm{M}_1)$ in such a way that $a=0$ and $q=0$ on $\mathrm{M}_{1} \setminus \mathrm{M}$.\\
We denote $\psi_{a_2}\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ and $\psi_{-a_1}\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ the solutions of (\ref{3.12}) respectively with $a=a_2$ and $a=-a_1$ given by (\ref{3.22}), and set
\begin{equation}\label{4.1}
\psi_a(x,t)=\psi_{a_2}(x,t)\psi_{-a_1}(x,t).
\end{equation} 
\begin{lemma}\label{L.4.1}
Let $T>0$. There exist $C>0$ such that for any $\theta_j\in \mathcal{V}(Q)$, $j=1,2$,

\begin{equation}\label{4.2}

+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(t,x)e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t r_{2,h}(\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1})(x,t) e^{-i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tr_{2,h}(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2(x,t)\overline{u}_1(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt \cr
= \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h \para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t+\mathscr{R}_h.
\end{multline}
In view of (\ref{4.7}) and (\ref{4.4}), we have
\begin{equation}\label{4.11}
\abs{\mathscr{R}_h}\leq C\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, by the trace theorem, we find
\begin{eqnarray}\label{4.12}
\bigg|\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}}\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}(f_{h}) \overline{g}_h \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t \bigg|
&\leq & \norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}} \norm{f_h}_{H^{1}(\Sigma)}\norm{g_h}_{L^2(\Sigma)}\cr
&\leq & Ch^{-3}\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}
-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}.
\end{eqnarray}
The estimate (\ref{4.2}) follows easily from (\ref{4.10}), (\ref{4.11}) and (\ref{4.12}).\\
This completes the proof of the Lemma.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{L.4.2} There exists $C>0$ such that for any $\Psi\in H^2 (S_y\mathrm{M}_{1})$, the following estimate

\Psi(\xi)  \,

We take two solutions to (\ref{3.11}) of the form

\begin{multline}\label{4.14}

\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t,r,\xi)

\, \mathrm{d} t\cr

\, \mathrm{d} t\cr

\Psi(\xi)  \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,

=2\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\int_0^T \frac{d}{dt}\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ t}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}

=2\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ T}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}-1}

By the support properties of the function $\phi$, we get that the left-hand side term in (\ref{4.14}) reads
\begin{multline*}
  \int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{T}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}-1}
\Psi(\xi)  \, \mathrm{d} \tau \,
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)=\cr
\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(s,y,\xi)ds}-1}
\Psi(\xi) \mu(y,\xi) \, 
\mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi).

Then, by (\ref{4.14}) and (\ref{4.2}) we get
\begin{multline}\label{4.15}
\abs{\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\para{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)}-1}
\Psi(\xi)  \,

 \leq C\para{h+h^{-2}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}} \norm{\Psi}_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_{1})}.

\begin{equation}\label{2.40}
\vert \int_{S\mathrm{M}} \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle  \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \vert \leq k^+  \int_{S\mathrm{M}}\vert H \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}u\vert^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}.
\end{equation}
Combining (\ref{2.40}), (\ref{2.39}) and (\ref{2.38}) with item (3) of Lemma \ref{L.2.2}, we find 
\begin{equation}\label{2.41}
(1-k^+)\int_{S\mathrm{M}}  \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}+(n-2) \int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert Hu\vert ^2  \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}\leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})}.
\end{equation}
For $k^+<1$ and $n\geq 2$, we deduce the estimate
\begin{equation}\label{2.42}
\int_{S\mathrm{M}}  \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \leq  C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})}.
\end{equation}
In view of the definition of $H$, in (\ref{2.30}), there exists a constant $C$ such that 
$$
\vert Hu \vert^2 \leq C  \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 .
$$ 
Using the item (2) of Lemma \ref{L.2.2} and (\ref{2.30}), we conclude that 
$$
\Vert f \Vert ^2_{L^2(S\mathrm{M})}=\int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert Hu \vert^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}\leq C \int_{S\mathrm{M}}  \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \leq  C\Vert\mathcal{I} f \Vert^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})},
 $$ and the Theorem \ref{theorem} is done. \\   
 Now, we come back to prove (\ref{2.38})-(\ref{2.39}) and (\ref{2.40}). First, we start with (\ref{2.40}). By (\ref{2.8}) we find
 \begin{equation}\label{2.43}
 \vert \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle \vert \leq K^+(x,\xi) \vert \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u(x,\xi) \vert^2,\quad \forall (x,\xi)\in S\mathrm{M}.
 \end{equation}
  Furthermore, the lemma \ref{L.2.3} combined with (\ref{2.43}) gives the following estimate
\begin{align} \label{2.44}
\int_{S \mathrm{M}} \vert \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle \vert \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} & \leq k^+ \int_{S \mathrm{M}}  \vert H\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u \vert^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} & \cr & \leq k^+ \int_{S \mathrm{M}}  \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1},
\end{align} 
This completes the proof of (\ref{2.40}).\\
We prove now (\ref{2.38}).  Since we have $Hu=-f$ and  $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}f=0$, then the Pestov's identity (\ref{2.31}) gives 
 \begin{equation}\label{2.45}
 \vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2+  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\textrm{div}}(V) + \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\textrm{div}}(W)- \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle=0.
 \end{equation}
 Avoiding eventual singularities of $u$  on $T \partial\mathrm{M}$, we will consider the variety $\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ defined by $$\mathrm{M}_{\rho}=\{x \in \mathrm{M},\quad d_\mathrm{g}(x,\partial \mathrm{M}) \geq \rho \},$$ where $\rho >0$. In some neighbourhood of $\partial \mathrm{M},$ the function $x \mapsto d_\mathrm{g}(x,\partial \mathrm{M})$ is smooth and $\partial \mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ is strictly convex for sufficiently small $\rho >0.$ The function $u$ is smooth on $S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ since $S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}\subset S\mathrm{M} \setminus S(\partial \mathrm{M})$. Integrating  (\ref{2.45}) over $S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ and using the formula divergence (\ref{2.27}) and (\ref{2.28}), we find 
 \begin{align*}
 \int_{S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}}\left[ \vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2- \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle\right]\, \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}= &
 -\int_{S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}} \left[ \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\textrm{div}}(V)  + \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\textrm{div}}(W)\right]\, \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \cr =&
  -\int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}} \langle V, \nu \rangle \quad d\sigma^{2n-2} -(n-2)\int_{S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}} \langle W, \xi \rangle \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1},
 \end{align*}
 where $\nu=\nu_{\rho}(x)$ is the unit vector of the outer normal to the boundary of $\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$.
 In view of (\ref{2.33}), we have 
 $$\langle W, \xi \rangle=\langle\xi,\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u\rangle ^2 = \vert Hu\vert ^2.$$
Hence, we obtain the equality 
\begin{equation}\label{2.46}
 \int_{S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}}\left[ \vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2- \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle+(n-2) \vert Hu\vert^2 \right]  \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}= -\int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}} \langle V, \nu \rangle \,d\sigma^{2n-2}.
\end{equation} 
Now, we wish pass to the limit as $\rho \rightarrow 0.$ We will apply the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem.  Denote by $\mathbb{\chi}_\rho$ the characteristic function of the set $S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ and by $p$  the projection $p : \partial S\mathrm{M} \longrightarrow  \partial S\mathrm{M}_\rho$, $p(x,\xi)=(x',\xi'),$ where $x'$ 
 is such that the geodesic $\gamma_{xx'}$ has length $\rho$ and intersects $\partial \mathrm{M}$ orthogonally at $x$ and $x'$, and $\xi'$ is obtained 
 by the parallel translation of the vector $\xi$ along $\gamma_{xx'}$. So the equality (\ref{2.46}) becomes 
 \begin{equation}\label{2.47}
 \int_{S\mathrm{M}}\left[ \vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2- \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle+(n-2) \vert Hu\vert ^2 \right] \mathbb{\chi}_\rho  \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}= -\int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}} \langle V, \nu \rangle p_* ( d\sigma^{2n-2}).
\end{equation} 
Note that all the integrands of (\ref{2.47}) are smooth on $S\mathrm{M} \setminus \partial S \mathrm{M}$ and so, they converge towards their values almost everywhere, when $\rho \rightarrow 0$. 
Since the functions $\vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2$ and $\vert Hu\vert ^2$  are positive and the second function satifies (\ref{2.43}), then the left side of (\ref{2.47}) converges as $\rho \rightarrow 0$.  To apply the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem in (\ref{2.47}), it remains to prove that $\vert \langle V, \nu \rangle p_*  \vert$ is bounded by a summable function on $\partial S \mathrm{M}$ which does not depend on $\rho$.\\
For $(x,\xi)\in \partial S\mathrm{M}$, we put
$$
\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u =\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u -\langle\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u ,\nu\rangle\nu,\quad \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u =\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u -\langle\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u,\xi\rangle\xi.
$$  
We see that
$$
\langle\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u ,\nu\rangle=\langle\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u,\xi\rangle=0.
$$
Then $\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}$ and $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}$ are in fact  differential operators on $\partial S\mathrm{M}$ and $\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}u$, $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}u$ are completely determined by the restriction $u_{|\partial S\mathrm{M}}$ of $u$ on $\partial S\mathrm{M}$.\\
For $(x,\xi)\in\partial S\mathrm{M}$, by a simple computation we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{2.48}
\langle V, \nu \rangle=\langle \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u , \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u  \rangle\langle\xi,\nu\rangle-\langle \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u , \xi\rangle\langle \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}  u ,\nu\rangle.
\end{equation}
From (\ref{2.34}), we can see that the derivatives $\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}u$ and $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} u$  are locally bounded on $\partial S\mathrm{M}$. It is important that the right-hand side of (\ref{2.48}) does not contain $\langle\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u,\nu\rangle$ and $\langle\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}u,\xi \rangle.$\\
Taking $\rho \rightarrow 0$ in the equality (\ref{2.46}), we have 
$$
\int_{S\mathrm{M}} \left[ \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2-\langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle+
(n-2) \vert Hu\vert ^2 \right]\,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}= -\int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}} \langle V, \nu \rangle \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}.
$$
Finally, It remains to prove the estimate (\ref{2.39}).  In view of the boundary condition $u=\mathcal{I} f$ on $\partial_+S\mathrm{M}$ and $u=0$ on $\partial_-S\mathrm{M}$ we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}} \langle V, \nu \rangle \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} &=\int_{\partial_+ S\mathrm{M}} \para{\langle \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} (\mathcal{I} f) , \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} (\mathcal{I} f)  \rangle\langle\xi,\nu\rangle-\langle \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} (\mathcal{I} f) , \xi\rangle\langle \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} (\mathcal{I} f) ,\nu\rangle} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}\cr
& :=\int_{\partial_+ S\mathrm{M}} \mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{I} f) \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} .
 \end{align*}
where $\mathcal{Q}u$ is a quadratic form in variables $\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}u$ and $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}u$ and hence, $\mathcal{Q}$ is a quadratic first-order  differential operator on the manifold $\partial_+ S \mathrm{M}$. Consequently, there exists a constant $C$ such that we have 
$$
\vert  \int_{\partial_+ S \mathrm{M}} \mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{I} f) \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} \vert \leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert ^2_{H^1(\partial_+ S \mathrm{M})}.
$$
 This completes the proof of the Theorem \ref{theorem}.

We define the Poisson kernel of $B(0,1)\subset T_y \mathrm{M}_1$, i-e.,
$$
P(\theta,\xi)=\frac{1-\abs{\theta}^2}{\alpha_n\abs{\theta-\xi}^n},\quad \theta\in B(0,1);\,\, \xi\in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
$$
For $0<\kappa<1$, we define $\Psi_\kappa: S_y\mathrm{M}_1\times S_y\mathrm{M}_1\to \mathbb{R}$ as
$$
\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi)=P(\kappa\theta,\xi).
$$
Let $P_0$ the Poisson kernel for the Euclidian unit ball $B_0(0,1)\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ i.e., 
$$
P_0(\hat{\theta},\hat{\xi})=\frac{1-\abs{\hat{\theta}}_0^2}{\alpha_n\abs{\hat{\theta}-\hat{\xi}}_0^n},\quad \hat{\theta}\in B_0(0,1);\,\, \hat{\xi}\in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}.
$$
where $\abs{\cdot}_0$ is the Euclidian norm of $\mathbb{R}^n$. From the well known properties of $P_0$, we have 
$$
\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}P_0(\kappa\hat{\theta},\hat{\xi}) d\omega_0(\hat{\xi})=1, \quad\textrm{for all}\, \kappa\in (0,1),\,\, \hat{\theta}\in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}.
$$
Let $\gamma=\sqrt{\mathrm{g}}:=(\gamma_{ij})$ be definite symetric positive matrix such that $\gamma^2=(g_{ij})$, then we get
$$
P(\theta,\xi)=\frac{1-\abs{\gamma^{-1}\theta}_0^2}{\alpha_n\abs{\gamma^{-1}\theta-\gamma^{-1}\xi}_0^n},\quad \theta,\xi\in S_y\mathrm{M}.
$$
we deduce from the change of variable $\hat{\xi}=\gamma^{-1}\xi$
\begin{eqnarray}\label{A1}
\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}P(\kappa\theta,\xi)d\omega_y(\xi)&=&\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}P_0(\kappa\gamma^{-1}\theta,\gamma^{-1}\xi)d\omega_y(\xi)\cr
&=&\frac{1}{\det\gamma}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}P_0(\kappa\gamma^{-1}\theta,\hat{\xi})(\det\gamma) d\omega_0(\hat{\xi})=1
\end{eqnarray}
This complete the proof of (\ref{4.18}).
Let now
$$
V_\theta=\set{\xi\in S_y\mathrm{M}_1,\,\,\abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}\leq (1-\kappa)^{1/2n}}.
$$
\begin{multline}\label{A.2}
\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) \abs{\theta-\xi}d\omega_y(\xi)\leq\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) \abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}d\omega_y(\xi)+(1-\kappa)\cr
\int_{V_\theta}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) \abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}d\omega_y(\xi)+\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1\backslash V_\theta}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) \abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}d\omega_y(\xi)+(1-\kappa)\cr
(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}+4(1-\kappa)^{1/2}+(1-\kappa)\leq C(1-\kappa)^{1/2n},
\end{multline}
and then we get (\ref{4.19}).\\
By a simple computation, we have
$$
\abs{\nabla_\xi^k P(\kappa\theta,\xi)}\leq C\frac{1-\kappa^2}{\abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}^{n+k}},\quad k=1,2,
$$
we deduce that
\begin{equation}
\norm{ \Psi_\kappa(\theta,\cdot)}^2_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_1)} \leq C\frac{1-\kappa^2}{(1-\kappa)^{n+4}}\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\frac{1-\kappa^2}{\abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}^n} d\omega_y(\xi)\leq 
\frac{C}{(1-\kappa)^{n+3}}.
\end{equation}
This complete the proof of (\ref{4.20}).
